steps.title: Answers
steps.body:
**Not from 2021 to 2022.** “Operating margin” is not a clean standalone metric for American Express: it does not report operating income, and its results are shaped by funding costs and credit-loss provisions as well as operating expenses. A useful proxy is **pretax income ÷ total revenues net of interest expense**.

- 2020: $4.296B ÷ $36.087B = **11.9%**
- 2021: $10.689B ÷ $42.380B = **25.2%**
- 2022: $9.585B ÷ $52.862B = **18.1%**

So the proxy margin improved substantially from 2020, but **contracted 7.1 percentage points in 2022 versus 2021**. The comparison is affected by credit losses: Amex recorded a $1.419B provision release in 2021, versus a $2.182B provision in 2022. (2022 Form 10-K, p. 93.)

steps.body:
**Not from 2021 to 2022.** AMEX’s reported statements do not present a separate “operating income” line, so operating margin is not a clean standalone metric here. For a card issuer, interest income and expense and credit-loss provisions are central to the business; excluding them can make an operating-margin comparison misleading.

As a rough proxy, pretax income divided by total revenues net of interest expense gives:

- **2022:** $9.585B ÷ $52.862B = **18.1%**
- **2021:** $10.689B ÷ $42.380B = **25.2%**
- **2020:** $4.296B ÷ $36.087B = **11.9%**

So the proxy margin improved substantially from 2020, but **declined in 2022 versus 2021**. The comparison is affected by credit-loss provisions: AMEX reported a **$1.419B provision release in 2021** and a **$2.182B provision in 2022**. (Filing pp. 44–46, 93.)
